metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Crosby v. National Foreign Trade Council

Opinion filed: 2000-06-19

Docket No.: 99-474

Citations:
• 147 L. Ed. 2d 352
• 120 S. Ct. 2288
• 530 U.S. 363
• 2000 U.S. LEXIS 4153

Case holding summaries:
• acknowledging that “the ‘nuances’ of ‘the foreign policy of the United States . . . are much more the province of the Executive Branch and Congress than of this Court’”
• The determination of “[w]hat is a sufficient obstacle” for purposes of preemption “is a matter of Judgment, to be informed by examining the federal statute as a whole and identifying its purpose and intended effects.”
• declaring it a “fundamental principle” of our republic “that Congress has the power to preempt state law”
• “We recognize, of course, that the categories of preemption are not ‘rigidly distinct.’” (quoting English v. Gen. Elec. Co., 496 U.S. 72, 79 n.5 (1990))
• "The `nuances' of the `foreign policy of the United States . . . are much more the province of the Executive Branch and Congress than of this Court.'"
• “[S]tate law is naturally preempted to the extent of any conflict with a federal statute.”
• overturning a Massachusetts statute preventing trade with Burma
• "[E]ven if Congress has not occupied the field, state law is naturally preempted to the extent of any conflict with a federal statute."
• expressing disapproval of acts that "compromise the very capacity of the President to speak for the nation with one voice in dealing with other governments"
• “A fundamental principle of the Constitution is that Congress has the power to preempt state law.”
• relying on statements by sponsors of act to support conclusion as to statutory construction
• "We leave for another day a consideration in this context of a presumption against preemption"
• “What is a sufficient obstacle is a matter of judgment, to be informed by examining the federal statute as a whole and identifying its purpose and intended effects . . . .”
• striking down a Massachusetts law that restricted state purchase of goods from companies in Burma (Myanmar) due to the state-sanctioned, mass genocide that continues to occur there
• stating that "[a] fundamental principle of the Constitution is that Congress has the power to preempt state law"
• stating that the agreements “illustrate” and “express[]” the 14 President’s policy, and quoting statements of officials regarding the policy underlying the 15 agreements, in describing “evidence” of the policy
• stating that the agreements “illustrate” and “express[]” the 14 President’s policy, and quoting statements of officials regarding the policy underlying the 15 agreements, in describing “evidence” of the policy
• recognizing that a federal law overrides any state law that frustrates the federal law's operation within its intended field
• stating that it is the duty of the Executive Branch to present a coherent position on behalf of the national economy
• stating when Congress intends federal law to "occupy the field," state law in that area is preempted
• “What is a sufficient obstacle is a matter of judgment, to be informed by examining the federal statute as a whole and identifying its purpose and intended effects”
• noting and relying on the Executive Branch’s direct remarks about a Massachusetts statute barring the 44 purchase of goods from those “doing business with Burma”
• "`[T]he peace of the whole ought not to be left at the disposal of a PART'" (quoting The Federalist No. 80, pp. 535-536 (J. Cooke ed. 1961) (A. Hamilton))
• "The Constitution's foreign affairs provisions have been long understood -38- to stand for the principle that power over foreign affairs is vested exclusively in the federal government."
• “‘[N]uances’ of the ‘foreign policy of the United States . . . are much more in the province of the Executive Branch and Congress than of this Court.’” (quoting Container Corp. of Am. v. Franchise Tax Bd., 463 U.S. 159, 196 (1983))
• “[T]he nuances of the foreign policy of the United States . . . are much more the province of the Executive Branch and Congress than of this Court.”
• "A failure to provide for preemption expressly may reflect nothing more than the settled character of implied preemption doctrine that courts will dependably apply."
• recognizing the importance of speaking with one voice to the international community in trade matters
• “[S]tate law is natu­ rally preempted to the extent of any conflict with a federal statute”
• acknowledging that "the 'nuances' of 'the foreign policy of the United States ... are much more the province of the Executive Branch and Congress than of this Court' "
• citing, inter alia, U.S. Const., art. VI, cl. 2; Gibbons v. Ogden, 9 Wheat. 1 (1824)
• "[w]e recognize, of course, that the categories of preemption are not "rigidly distinct"
• discussing express, conflict, and field preemption
• invalidating a Massachusetts statute which stood as an obstacle to a Con- gressional act imposing sanctions on Burma
• noting that the presumption against preemption may be overcome where state law "presents a sufficient obstacle to the full accomplishment of Congress's objectives under the federal [enactment] to find it preempted"
• explaining that a “state law must yield” if “the purpose -12- of [a federal law] cannot otherwise be accomplished—if its operation within its chosen field else must be frustrated”
• holding State’s measure preempted by federal statute that conferred on the Presi- dent “discretion to exercise economic leverage . . . with an eye toward national security”
• "[T]he entire scheme of the statute must of course be considered and that which needs must be implied is of no less force that that which is expressed."
• facial, conflict-obstacle challenge: Massachusetts law barring companies from doing business with Burma presents obstacle to federal Foreign Commerce Clause
• Court "acknowledged that the nuances of the foreign policy of the United States ... are much more the province of the Executive Branch and Congress than of this Court" in litigation challenging state legislation regulating private corporations engaged in foreign commerce
• acknowledging that “the ‘nuances’ of ‘the foreign policy of the United States . . . are much more the province of the Executive Branch and Congress than of this Court’ ”
• "The State's inference of congressional intent is unwarranted here, therefore, simply because the silence of Congress is ambiguous."
• “The State’s inference of congressional intent is unwarranted here, therefore, simply because the silence of Congress is ambiguous.”
• rejecting a similar argument in relation to the Uruguay Round Agreements Act in using WTO proceedings as evidence in construing an Act of Congress
